title: What We Choose
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 16 of 40
content:
What I chose mattered more than what the road expected.

The final governor refused to meet in a tea house. He demanded that Iroh come to the old military compound outside the city, where the gates still bore the emblem of the previous regime.

“He wants you to remember who you were,” I said.

“Perhaps.”

“Do you?”

Iroh looked at the compound. “Every day.”

The governor greeted him with armed guards and a table covered in maps. He did not offer tea.

“The Fire Nation will not withdraw from this region,” the governor said.

“The Fire Nation is withdrawing,” Iroh replied.

“You speak as though you command it.”

“I speak as someone who has learned the cost of believing command is the same as wisdom.”

The governor laughed. “You grew soft.”

Iroh's face did not change.

I stood near the door with the tea chest. My hands wanted to move. My body wanted to step between them. Iroh had asked me to remain, not to intervene.

The meeting lasted hours. The governor accused Iroh of abandoning his nation. Iroh admitted that he had served a system that caused harm. The governor called that weakness. Iroh called it responsibility.

At last, the governor pushed the maps away.

“You expect me to trust the people who defeated us?” he asked.

“No,” Iroh said. “I expect you to stop making fear into a government.”

The governor's guards reached for their weapons.

Iroh moved before I could think. Fire bloomed in his palm, controlled and bright. He did not strike. He only placed the flame between the governor and the maps.

“If you wish to fight,” he said, “you will fight me. But you will not use these people as shields.”

The room went silent.

The governor lowered his hand.

The agreement was signed before sunset.

Outside the compound, I found Iroh sitting on a stone step. His hands were clasped between his knees.

“You were magnificent,” I said.

“I was angry.”

“Both can be true.”

He looked toward the horizon. “Fire is easy to mistake for power. Sometimes it is only emotion with a direction.”

“You controlled it.”

“I chose not to burn the room.”

“That seems important.”

“It is a low standard.”

“It is still a choice.”

I sat beside him.

“The journey is ending,” I said.

“Yes.”

“You will return to Ba Sing Se.”

“Yes.”

“And I will return with you.”

Iroh turned his head.

“If you want me,” I said.

“I have wanted you since you entered the shop carrying the rain.”

“That sounds like an exaggeration.”

“It is a poetic truth.”

“You are impossible.”

“You have said this many times.”

I leaned against his shoulder. “I have also said I love you.”

“That is my favorite repetition.”

The return journey took six days. There were fewer negotiations and more quiet mornings. I stopped at springs, villages, and one shrine where an elderly monk insisted that Iroh had the posture of a man who needed to rest.

“He is correct,” I said.

“He is a stranger.”

“He is observant.”

“You are forming a conspiracy.”

“Against your sleep schedule.”

Iroh slept late the next morning. I made tea. It was not as good as his, but he drank it.

“You are improving,” he said.

“You sound surprised.”

“I am proud.”

The word settled over me.

“I don’t want to be your student forever,” I said.

“Then be my partner.”

I looked at him.

Iroh set down his cup. “The distinction is important.”

“Is that a proposal?”

“It is an invitation.”

“To what?”

“To walk beside me without believing you must follow.”

I reached across the small table. He took my hand.

“Yes,” I said.

“To the invitation?”

“To you.”

He kissed me beside the road, with the cart waiting and the tea cooling beside it.

When Ba Sing Se finally appeared beyond the fields, my chest tightened. The city looked the same from a distance: walls, towers, green roofs, lanterns.

But I had changed.

The Jasmine Dragon waited somewhere inside.

So did home.

Before entering the city, Iroh stopped the cart beside a field of yellow flowers. He climbed down and walked a short distance away, looking toward the walls.

“What are you doing?” I asked.

“Saying goodbye to the road.”

“We are not leaving the road forever.”

“No. But it will be different when we return.”

I stood beside him. The wind moved through the flowers in slow waves.

“I thought I would feel relieved,” I said.

“Do you not?”

“I do. I also feel sad.”

“Relief and sadness are not enemies.”

“You have an answer for everything.”

“I have had many years to collect them.”

“Have you collected any that are useful?”

“A few.”

He reached for my hand.

“The journey showed me something,” he said. “I have spent years believing that if I returned to the places I harmed, I could make them balance. But the world does not balance so neatly.”

“What will you do instead?”

“I will help where I can. I will accept that some wounds are not mine to close. I will keep the tea shop open.”

“And us?”

Iroh's thumb moved over my knuckles. “I will not ask you to become proof of my redemption.”

“Good.”

“I will ask you to continue being yourself near me, if you wish.”

“That sounds difficult.”

“It is also my favorite plan.”

I leaned against him.

“I want to continue,” I said.

“Then we will.”

The city gates opened as the sun lowered. Guards checked the cart's documents. One recognized Iroh and stood straighter. Iroh returned the greeting without accepting the title.

Inside the walls, the streets felt narrower than I remembered. The market noise rose around me. People turned to watch the cart. Some recognized Iroh. Some recognized me.

“We are being observed,” I said.

“We are interesting.”

“You are interesting.”

“You are carrying the damaged tea chest.”

“A compelling spectacle.”

He drove toward the shop. The green dragon sign appeared between rooftops.

The Jasmine Dragon looked smaller than it had when I left. The room above it seemed impossibly close. I had been away less than a month, but the distance had changed the meaning of every step.

Iroh unlocked the door.

The kettle whistled immediately.

“It missed you,” I said.

“It is demanding attention.”

“Some things do.”

He looked at me. “Yes.”

Inside, the substitute tea master had left the shelves organized and the counters polished. The white lotus tile sat beside the register. My cup with my name was wrapped in cloth.

Iroh unwrapped it and handed it to me.

“It survived,” he said.

“You were worried?”

“I was practical.”

“You were worried.”

“Perhaps.”

I placed the cup at the corner table. He set the white lotus beside it.

“A good position,” I said.

“An excellent one.”

The shop lights came on. Dust moved through the warm air.

I and Iroh stood in the doorway to the room above the shop.

“Tomorrow,” he said, “we reopen.”

“Tomorrow.”

“Tonight?”

I took his hand. “Tonight, we rest.”

His eyes softened.

The road had asked me to be useful, brave, and patient. The shop asked only that I return.

We climbed the stairs together.

The room above the shop held the scent of jasmine and dust. My books were still on the shelf. The white lotus tile remained beside the window. Iroh's travel bag landed near the door with a tired thump.

“The bed looks smaller,” I said.

“The room has not changed.”

“We have.”

Iroh looked around. “Yes.”

I opened the balcony doors. The city sounded familiar now: carts, bells, distant voices, the kettle downstairs preparing to complain.

“I thought coming back would feel like an ending,” I said.

“It can be a beginning too.”

“You say that about everything.”

“Beginnings are abundant.”

I turned toward him. “Are you tired?”

“Very.”

“Do you want tea?”

“Always.”

We went downstairs together. Iroh brewed the jasmine blend while I sat at the counter. His hands moved automatically, but his eyes kept returning to me.

“You are staring,” I said.

“I am confirming that you are here.”

“I am.”

“Good.”

I took the cup he offered. The first sip tasted like the day I met him and all the days that had followed.

“Still better than the pastry?” he asked.

“The pastry was important.”

“But the tea?”

I lifted the cup. “The tea stayed.”

Iroh smiled.

He took my cup and refilled it before his own.

“You are learning,” I said.

“I have an excellent teacher.”

“You mean the tea.”

“I mean you.”

The shop below began to stir.

Iroh set the cup down and kissed my forehead. Then the two of us went downstairs to meet the morning.

The kettle whistled. The street woke. We opened the shop together.

The first customer was already waiting outside with an umbrella and a story.

Iroh welcomed them in.

Iroh welcomed them in.

Iroh set the cup down and kissed my forehead. Then the two of us went downstairs to meet the morning.
